name: Learn: RBAC & Certificates
description: Master Kubernetes authorization step by step — Roles, ClusterRoles, bindings, ServiceAccounts, least-privilege, and approving a CSR. Then prove it in the cka-006 exam.
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration (25%). Goal: create Roles/ClusterRoles and bindings, grant ServiceAccounts, scope least-privilege with resourceNames, and approve a CSR — RBAC & cert tasks that appear on almost every CKA.

questions.title: Role + RoleBinding (namespaced)
questions.teach:
**RBAC** decides who can do what. A **Role** lists allowed *verbs* on *resources* **within one namespace**. A **RoleBinding** grants a Role to one or more *subjects*.

The chain: `subject → RoleBinding → Role → verbs on resources`.

**Verbs:** `get`, `list`, `watch`, `create`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`, `deletecollection` (and `*` for all). `get`/`list`/`watch` are the read trio; mutating verbs are `create`/`update`/`patch`/`delete`.

**Subject kinds:** `User`, `Group`, or `ServiceAccount`. Users/Groups are just strings the authenticator supplies — Kubernetes has no User object. A RoleBinding may list several subjects at once.

**Rules shape:** a rule is `apiGroups` + `resources` + `verbs` (the core group is `""`, e.g. pods/services/configmaps). You can also name **subresources** like `pods/log`, `pods/exec`, `pods/status`.

**Create vs declare:**
- Imperative: `kubectl create role NAME --verb=... --resource=...` and `kubectl create rolebinding NAME --role=... --user=... / --group=... / --serviceaccount=ns:name`.
- Declarative YAML gives you full control (multiple rules, apiGroups, resourceNames).

**Gotchas:**
- Test effective access with `kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=<user> -n <ns>` — answers `yes`/`no` without logging in. Add `--as-group=` for a group, `--list` to dump all perms.
- A RoleBinding lives in a namespace and only grants access **in that namespace**, even though it can reference a ClusterRole.
- Deleting the RoleBinding (not the Role) is what revokes access; both must exist for access to work.
- `apiGroups` matters: `deployments` are in `apps`, not the core group — omitting the group silently grants nothing.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `rbac-learn`, create a Role `pod-reader` allowing `get,list,watch` on `pods`, and a RoleBinding granting it to user `dev`.

Target: `kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=dev -n rbac-learn` → `yes`.
questions.hint: `kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n rbac-learn`, then `kubectl create rolebinding dev-pr --role=pod-reader --user=dev -n rbac-learn`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n rbac-learn
kubectl create rolebinding dev-pr --role=pod-reader --user=dev -n rbac-learn
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> yes

verification.description: user 'dev' can list pods in rbac-learn

questions.title: ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-scoped)
questions.teach:
Some resources (nodes, persistentvolumes, namespaces, clusterroles) are **cluster-scoped** — they live outside any namespace, so a namespaced Role can't grant access to them. A **ClusterRole** holds the rules; a **ClusterRoleBinding** grants them cluster-wide.

Rule of thumb:
- namespaced resource, one namespace → Role + RoleBinding
- cluster-scoped resource, OR a namespaced resource across *all* namespaces → ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding

**The key cross-over (very exam-relevant):** a **RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole**. This reuses one ClusterRole's rules but **scopes them to the RoleBinding's namespace** — the standard pattern for "give dev admin, but only in team-a". The reverse is impossible: a ClusterRoleBinding always grants cluster-wide.

**Other ClusterRole features:**
- `nonResourceURLs` (e.g. `/healthz`, `/metrics`) can only be granted via a ClusterRole, never a Role.
- **Aggregation:** a ClusterRole with an `aggregationRule` (label selector) auto-merges rules from other ClusterRoles carrying the matching label — how the built-in `admin`/`edit`/`view` roles get extended.
- Built-in ClusterRoles `cluster-admin`, `admin`, `edit`, `view` already exist — bind them instead of reinventing.

**Gotchas:**
- `kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=dev` with no `-n` checks cluster scope; a namespaced check won't reveal a ClusterRoleBinding grant correctly for cluster resources.
- A ClusterRole alone grants nothing until something binds it.
questions.prompt:
Create a ClusterRole `node-reader` allowing `get,list` on `nodes`, and a ClusterRoleBinding granting it to user `dev`.

Target: `kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=dev` → `yes`.
questions.hint: `kubectl create clusterrole node-reader --verb=get,list --resource=nodes`, then `kubectl create clusterrolebinding dev-nr --clusterrole=node-reader --user=dev`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create clusterrole node-reader --verb=get,list --resource=nodes
kubectl create clusterrolebinding dev-nr --clusterrole=node-reader --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=dev   # -> yes

questions.title: ServiceAccount identity
questions.teach:
Users are for humans; **ServiceAccounts** are identities for *workloads* (pods). A pod runs as a ServiceAccount and gets a token to call the API. You grant a SA permissions the same way — bind a Role or ClusterRole to it.

**The two names you'll mix up:**
- In a binding's `subjects`: `kind: ServiceAccount`, `name: ci`, `namespace: rbac-learn`.
- In `auth can-i --as=` and in RBAC rules: the full form `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>` (here `system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci`). The group `system:serviceaccounts:<namespace>` covers all SAs in a namespace.
- CLI shortcut: `kubectl create rolebinding ... --serviceaccount=<ns>:<name>` (colon, not the full `system:` prefix).

**Attaching a SA to a pod:** set `spec.serviceAccountName` on the pod/template. Every namespace has a `default` SA used when none is specified.

**Tokens (1.24+):**
- No auto-generated Secret token anymore. Get a short-lived token with `kubectl create token <sa>` (TokenRequest API).
- For a long-lived token, create a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` annotated with `kubernetes.io/service-account.name`.
- `automountServiceAccountToken: false` (on SA or pod) stops mounting the token into the pod.

**Gotchas:**
- A SA with no binding has essentially no API permissions — the `default` SA is intentionally powerless.
- Binding namespace matters: a RoleBinding only grants in its own namespace even if the SA lives elsewhere.
questions.prompt:
In `rbac-learn`, create a ServiceAccount `ci`, then bind the existing `pod-reader` Role to it with a RoleBinding.

Target: `kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci -n rbac-learn` → `yes`.
questions.hint: `kubectl create sa ci -n rbac-learn`, then `kubectl create rolebinding ci-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=rbac-learn:ci -n rbac-learn`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create sa ci -n rbac-learn
kubectl create rolebinding ci-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=rbac-learn:ci -n rbac-learn
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci -n rbac-learn   # -> yes

verification.description: ServiceAccount ci can list pods in rbac-learn

questions.title: Least privilege with resourceNames
questions.teach:
Least privilege means granting the *minimum* needed. Beyond verbs+resources, a Role can restrict to **specific object names** via `resourceNames` — e.g. read only *one* ConfigMap, not all of them.

**How `resourceNames` behaves (the classic trap):**
- It works for verbs that act on a *named* object: `get`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`.
- It **cannot** restrict `list`, `watch`, `create`, or `deletecollection` — these operate on a collection (or, for create, the name isn't known yet), so a rule with `resourceNames` simply won't authorize them. If you need `list`, the user sees *all* objects of that type.

**CLI:** `kubectl create role NAME --verb=get --resource=configmaps --resource-name=app-config` (repeat `--resource-name` for several names). In YAML it's a `resourceNames: [app-config]` list inside the rule.

**Other least-privilege levers:**
- Narrow `verbs` (read-only trio vs mutating verbs).
- Narrow `resources` and use **subresources** (`pods/log`, `pods/exec`) to allow logs without full pod access.
- Prefer namespaced Role over ClusterRole; prefer binding a ClusterRole via a RoleBinding to confine scope.

**Gotchas:**
- Verify both the allow AND the deny: `can-i get configmaps/app-config --as=dev` → yes, `.../other-config` → no.
- `resourceNames` is ANDed with the rule — the subject still needs the verb+resource granted in the same rule.
questions.prompt:
Two ConfigMaps exist in `rbac-learn`: `app-config` and `other-config`. Create a Role + RoleBinding so user `dev` can `get` **only** `app-config`.

Target: `can-i get configmaps/app-config --as=dev` → `yes`, but `can-i get configmaps/other-config --as=dev` → `no`.
questions.hint: `kubectl create role cm-reader --verb=get --resource=configmaps --resource-name=app-config -n rbac-learn`, then bind it to `dev`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create role cm-reader --verb=get --resource=configmaps --resource-name=app-config -n rbac-learn
kubectl create rolebinding dev-cm --role=cm-reader --user=dev -n rbac-learn
kubectl auth can-i get configmaps/app-config  --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> yes
kubectl auth can-i get configmaps/other-config --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> no

verification.description: dev can get app-config but NOT other-config

questions.title: Approve a CertificateSigningRequest
questions.teach:
To give a *new human user* cluster access you issue them a client certificate: they generate a key + CSR, submit a **CertificateSigningRequest** object, an admin **approves** it, the signer issues the cert, and it goes into their kubeconfig. Kubernetes authenticates the user by the cert's **CN** (username) and **O** (groups).

**The full flow:**
1. `openssl genrsa` + `openssl req -new` → a `.csr`, with `/CN=dev/O=devs`.
2. Create a CSR object (`certificates.k8s.io/v1`) with `spec.request` = base64 of the PEM, and critically `spec.signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client` plus `spec.usages: [client auth]`.
3. `kubectl certificate approve <name>` (or `deny`) — an admin decision.
4. `kubectl get csr <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' | base64 -d` to retrieve the issued cert.

**Signer names matter:**
- `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client` — client certs for users (most common on exam).
- `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet`, `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving`, `kubernetes.io/legacy-unknown`.

**Gotchas:**
- Approving a CSR only authenticates (proves identity) — it grants **no permissions**. You still need a RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding to the CN/O to authorize anything.
- A `Pending` CSR has no `.status.certificate`; after approval the condition reads `Approved,Issued`.
- `approve`/`deny` are terminal — you can't flip an already-decided CSR; recreate it.
- Wrong/missing `usages` (`client auth`) or `signerName` means it won't issue a usable client cert.

A CSR named `learn-dev` has already been submitted and is **Pending** — your job is to approve it.
questions.prompt:
Approve the pending CSR named `learn-dev`.

Target: `kubectl get csr learn-dev` shows condition `Approved,Issued`.
questions.hint: `kubectl get csr` to see it Pending, then `kubectl certificate approve learn-dev`.
questions.solution:
kubectl get csr
kubectl certificate approve learn-dev
kubectl get csr learn-dev   # Approved,Issued
